content:
After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing an American offer to discuss postwar European security — and Moscow is using that diplomatic opening to reaffirm the tough demands President Vladimir Putin put forward before the start of his full-scale invasion. The proposal to discuss broader security arrangements for Europe was floated by US President Donald Trump's envoys, and it has worried Ukraine and its Western allies, who fear it will play into Moscow's hands and weaken NATO. The Kremlin, by contrast, has strongly backed the idea, describing a review of the broader European security framework as vital for a settlement of Europe's most devastating conflict since World War II.

Putin discussed the Ukrainian conflict with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in their first trilateral meeting. That encounter had fuelled fears in Kyiv that the three leaders could discuss a possible settlement without Ukraine's participation. According to [the Associated Press](https://www.asiaone.com/world/russia-grasps-us-offer-european-security-revive-old-demands), it was in that setting that the wider security question moved to the centre of the diplomacy. For background on that meeting, see our report on the [first trilateral summit in Shenzhen](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19).

The demands Moscow is reviving date back to December 2021, when Russia submitted draft agreements to the United States and NATO, two months before the invasion. In those documents, Russia demanded that Washington and its allies pledge to exclude NATO's expansion to Ukraine, Georgia or any other nation that was once part of the Soviet Union. Moscow also demanded that the US and its allies commit not to deploy weapons or conduct any military activities in Ukraine and other ex-Soviet nations. The documents further obliged the alliance not to station any troops in areas where they were not present in 1997 — before NATO moved to incorporate former Soviet-bloc countries and ex-Soviet republics. They also suggested a freeze on patrols by Russian and US warships and bombers near each other's borders, efforts to reduce the risk of incidents involving Russian and NATO warships and aircraft, primarily in the Baltic and the Black seas, a reduction in the scope of military drills, and greater transparency and other confidence-building measures. NATO allies rejected the Russian demands as a nonstarter.

Putin has described the West's refusal to consider those proposals as the main reason behind his decision to send troops into Ukraine on February 24, 2022, arguing that he had to act to fend off a major threat to Russia's national security. Ukraine and its allies denounce the invasion as an unprovoked act of aggression. Speaking after the meeting with Xi and Trump, Putin reaffirmed his criticism of the West for failing to take Moscow's complaints about NATO's expansion into account. "They just spat at our opinion," he said. He bluntly rejected the European response to Moscow's plans, calling it "political diarrhoea" and "nonsense," and saying that "everybody understands that we don't strive for a war with Europe."

At the same time, Putin said Russia is open to discussing the continent's security arrangements with the Europeans, as the US has suggested, and scoffed at what he called "hysterics in some European capitals" over Washington's offer. "We understand that it makes no sense to discuss issues related to security in Europe without the Europeans," he declared, adding that Moscow had invited a European delegation to visit and state its negotiating position before deciding on the date and format of further talks on Ukraine. He also made clear that Russia is ready to search for compromise but will not budge on its key demands, and he has sternly warned that Russia will not accept the deployment of any European troops into Ukraine after the hostilities end, saying Moscow would regard such contingents as legitimate targets.

Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said that during talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on November 12 in the Kremlin, Putin reminded them of Moscow's 2021 security proposals, noting that they envisioned the pullback of NATO forces from Central and Eastern Europe. Ushakov said the Kremlin would now update them with "fresh considerations." That meeting was part of the shuttle diplomacy that has accelerated this month; Kushner's parallel engagement with Kyiv is covered in our report on the [Ukraine talks in Berlin](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/kushner-ukraine-talks-progress-zelenskyy-missiles-november-2026).

Ukraine and its allies fear the security talks will benefit Moscow. European leaders worry that Putin could persuade Trump to support a peace settlement that would weaken not only Ukraine but broader European security. The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands. "If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us," she said at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin earlier this month. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also warned that the US proposal to discuss a new security framework for Europe before the war's end could be dangerous, arguing that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent's borders. He has reiterated that NATO membership remains Ukraine's clearest security guarantee, and that any alternative assurances must be backed by concrete commitments and remain valid beyond Trump's presidency.

There are, however, voices on both sides who see room for manoeuvre. Kushner said after meeting Zelenskyy and European leaders on Thursday in Berlin that Trump wants to make a deal with Europe "by his side" and is not looking to impose a unilateral agreement. He emphasised that Trump is "open" to NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine and added that he believes Russia is "comfortable" with the allies offering such assurances to Kyiv. Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said. Alexei Naumov, a pro-Kremlin political commentator, argued that the Russian demands represent an initial bargaining position that could become more flexible during talks. "Between maintaining the current status quo and the full realisation of Russia's demands, there is a vast space for compromise: mutual arms limitations, agreements regarding the deployment of military infrastructure, the parameters for a future Ukrainian military, security guarantees, and mechanisms to monitor their implementation," he said in a commentary. "Russia is currently negotiating from a position of strength, but that does not at all mean there will be no compromises."

Independent analysts are more cautious. Tatiana Stanovaya, an expert at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, said that "for the first time since 2022, Moscow sees a concrete opening for negotiations that could address what it calls the 'root causes' of the war." But she added that the Kremlin's expectations for this round are low, and that if the talks fail, Russia is prepared to keep fighting until another opening presents itself. Stanovaya also noted that Putin wants Europe to accept that Russia will have to be part of any negotiation on European security, and predicted the prospective talks will fuel differences among the allies. "I expect the process to deepen divisions within Europe, with little prospect of concrete results," she said. Russia expert Mark Galeotti, who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, said Moscow's set of demands could reflect "the classic attempt to start with a very, very exaggeratedly ambitious list of proposals with the expectation that you get haggled down." Galeotti also suggested Putin could be searching for a face-saving way to end the war without achieving the land gains in Ukraine that he had sought.

What happens next is still unclear, and the obstacles go beyond the NATO question. Even without the wider dispute over Europe's security architecture, the negotiations face a major hurdle over territory: Putin continues to insist that Ukraine surrender the parts of the Donbas region it still controls, a concession Zelenskyy has rejected. US-mediated negotiations involving Russia and Ukraine resumed in Abu Dhabi during November, producing an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no comprehensive peace settlement, and the date and format of the next round have not been settled. Witkoff indicated after his Moscow talks that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round, but the Kremlin later said a final decision on European participation had not been taken. For now, the most significant development may be the one the Kremlin itself is celebrating: after almost five years of war, the question of European security — the issue Moscow says was at the root of the conflict — is back on the negotiating agenda, on terms Russia helped to set.
summary: Moscow is seizing on a US proposal to discuss the future of European security to put back on the table the sweeping demands it issued weeks before invading Ukraine — no further NATO enlargement, no Western troops or weapons in former Soviet states, and a rollback of the alliance's military footprint in Central and Eastern Europe.
title: Russia revives its 2021 NATO demands as US floats talks on Europe's security
